Hex is base 16, using the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F for 10 to 15. Because 16 equals 2⁴, one hex digit represents exactly one nibble, so any byte can be written as two hex digits.

Programmers use hex because it is much shorter than binary, easier to read and less error-prone, and it converts directly to binary. Common uses include colour codes, MAC addresses and memory addresses.

Binary to hex: split into nibbles and convert each to a hex digit. Hex to binary: write each digit as 4 bits.

Denary to hex: divide by 16, the quotient is the first digit and the remainder the second (or go via binary). Hex to denary: multiply the first digit by 16 and add the second.
